name: Yoruba
notes: Standard Yoruba. Seven oral vowels /i e ɛ a ɔ o u/ (⟨i e ẹ a ọ o u⟩) and five nasal vowels /ĩ ɛ̃ ã ɔ̃ ũ/; there are no nasal counterparts of /e/ and /o/, which is why ⟨en⟩ and ⟨on⟩ are NOT nasal-vowel spellings. ⟨p⟩ = the labial-velar stop /k͡p/, ⟨gb⟩ = /ɡ͡b/, ⟨ẹ⟩ = /ɛ/, ⟨ọ⟩ = /ɔ/, ⟨ṣ⟩ = /ʃ/, ⟨j⟩ = /dʒ/ (also analysed as the palatal stop /ɟ/). /r/ is phonetically an alveolar tap [ɾ], not a trill (Akinlabi 2004; also Bamgboṣe, A. (1966) 'A Grammar of Yoruba', p.7). TONE: Yoruba has three level tones — high, mid, low — and the orthography writes them on the vowel with an acute, nothing, and a grave respectively, so tone is recoverable from spelling and the spec emits it. High is ◌́, low is ◌̀, and an orthographically unmarked vowel is MID, emitted with the IPA mid-tone diacritic ◌̄ rather than left bare: mid is a specified tone in Yoruba, not the absence of one (Bamgboṣe 1966; Akinlabi 2004). NASALISATION AFTER A NASAL ONSET: allophone_rules nasalise /i a ɔ u/ after ⟨m⟩ or ⟨n⟩; see YO_NASAL_AFTER_NASAL_ONSET_I_MID for the statement and its sources. /ɛ/ is excluded: phonemic /ɛ̃/ is confined to a single word in the source, and the gold agrees at 5.45% (3 of 55 contexts). The counter-examples that stay oral are not a loanword stratum — they are core native vocabulary: the numerals mẹfa/mẹta/mẹrin/mẹjọ/mẹwaa and their derivatives account for the oral-/ɛ/ exceptions, and 82 distinct words carry oral /a/ after a nasal onset, native items like Olodumare, Eledumare, Oṣumare, amala, awọsanma, majele, magun, mariwo, imale and nama among them. That is lexical knowledge a grapheme spec does not have, and it belongs to a caller-supplied lexicon. NASAL VOWELS: ⟨n⟩ that follows one of the five nasalisable vowels and is not itself followed by a vowel spells nasalisation of that vowel and is not a consonant of its own — ⟨un⟩ /ũ/, ⟨in⟩ /ĩ/, ⟨an⟩ /ã/, ⟨ọn⟩ /ɔ̃/, ⟨ẹn⟩ /ɛ̃/. Before a vowel the same ⟨n⟩ is an ordinary onset /n/, which the positional_graphemes before_vowel overrides restore (⟨ana⟩ /ānā/, not */ãā/). The tone diacritic is written AFTER the nasalisation tilde so the result composes to the same NFC string as the standard notation (ũ + ́ = ṹ). SYLLABIC NASAL: Yoruba permits only open syllables (Adesola, O., 'Yoruba: A Grammar Sketch', Afranaph, §2.1.2, https://afranaphproject.afranaphdatabase.com/images/stories/downloads/casefiles/YorubaGS.pdf), so an ⟨n⟩ followed by a consonant is never a coda. It is one of two things: the nasalisation mark of the preceding vowel, or a syllable nucleus of its own — a syllabic nasal that carries its own tone (same work, p. 2 n. 4: 'Syllabic nasals can also bear tones in Yoruba'). The nasal-vowel reading needs a vowel that HAS a nasal counterpart, and Yoruba has only /ĩ ɛ̃ ã ɔ̃ ũ/ (same work, chart 3). Where that reading is unavailable the syllabic reading is the only one left, and the spec applies it there and nowhere else: ⟨n⟩ before a consonant with no preceding vowel (⟨nkọ⟩, ⟨njẹ⟩, ⟨nnkan⟩) and after ⟨e⟩ or ⟨o⟩, which have no nasal counterpart (⟨Aderonkẹ⟩, ⟨otente⟩). Maximal munch does the selection on its own — ⟨an in ọn un ẹn⟩ are longer graphemes and win, so a single ⟨n⟩ + before_consonant override reaches exactly the residue. The wikipron gold agrees without exception in that residue: word-initial ⟨n⟩+C is a velar nasal in 11 of 11 words, ⟨n⟩ after a consonant in 5 of 5, ⟨on⟩+C in 28 of 28 and ⟨en⟩+C in 5 of 5. PLACE: the descriptive literature calls the syllabic nasal homorganic with what follows, but the spec emits one velar and does not guess a place from the spelling, for two measured reasons. Standard Yoruba already spells the labial variant ⟨m⟩ (⟨òrombó⟩, same work p. 2 n. 4), so an orthographic ⟨n⟩ before a labial is not evidence of a labial nasal; and the wikipron gold transcribes a velar in every nasal-before-consonant environment it has, including 23 words where the spelling is ⟨n⟩ before ⟨b p f⟩ (⟨Ganbia⟩ ɡáŋ́bíà, ⟨danpara⟩ dáŋ̀k͡pá, ⟨anfaani⟩ àŋ̀fàànĩ́) and 19 where the spelling is ⟨m⟩ before a consonant (⟨Abimbọla⟩ ābíŋ̄bɔ́lá, ⟨Gambari⟩ ɡàŋ̀bàɾí). Zero words in the gold transcribe a labial or alveolar nasal in that position. Emitting [m̩] before labials would therefore be a phonetic refinement this gold cannot confirm and would contradict in 42 words. The syllabicity is written with ◌̩, matching the ⟨ń⟩ and ⟨ǹ⟩ entries the spec already shipped; the gold writes a bare ŋ with a tone mark instead, which costs 0.0017 PER on the wikipron row (0.3828 with the mark, 0.3811 without) — a notation convention, not an error. STILL NOT MODELLED: ⟨n⟩ before a consonant after ⟨a i ọ u ẹ⟩, where both readings are available and the gold genuinely splits — 109 words take the syllabic nasal against 375 that take the nasal vowel, and no orthographic condition separates them, so the majority nasal-vowel reading is kept. That residue is the bulk of the gold's ŋ. KNOWN GAPS, not modelled: (1) downstep, which the wikipron gold marks and the orthography does not record, so it is not recoverable from spelling; (3) the ⟨ị⟩ and ⟨ụ⟩ of the extended orthography some gold entries use are unmapped and therefore dropped. GOLD CONVENTION: the vox_communis 'yo' row is epitran-derived — a machine gold with no tone and inconsistent nasal-vowel handling — so it scores AGREEMENT with epitran, not accuracy, and emitting tone necessarily moves that row a long way. Rank Yoruba on the wikipron row. The syllabic-nasal rule is a worked example of the divergence: that row has 504 words in the same environment as the 536 that trigger it and the symbol ŋ does not occur anywhere in the vox_communis 'yo' gold at all, so the rule can only cost that row — it moves 0.6341 to 0.6392 while moving wikipron 0.3832 to 0.3828. See docs/languages/yo.md. KNOWN GAP, NOT MODELLED: a written geminate vowel after a nasal onset (⟨maapu⟩, ⟨ibomii⟩) does not reliably nasalise both vowel slots. The wikipron gold has 28 such words; the engine nasalises the first slot and leaves the second oral in 10 of them where the gold nasalises both (⟨ibomii⟩ gold ībòmĩ́ĩ̀, engine ībōmĩ̄ī), and it nasalises the first slot in 4 more where the gold is oral throughout (⟨maapu⟩ gold máàk͡pù, engine mã̄ākpū). The gap is therefore two-sided — under-application and over-application in comparable numbers — which is what makes it unsafe to close by propagation. A prior round added rules propagating the first vowel's nasality onto an identical second vowel, but that does not hold up: scoped to the four nasalisable target vowels /i a ɔ u/ the gold splits (nasal,nasal) 9 against (oral,oral) 8 — a coin flip, not a majority — and the wikipron gold for the flagship example, maapu, is itself oral in both vowels ('m á à k͡p ù'). The rules also only ever fired because wikipron headwords carry no tone diacritics, so the tone-default rule assigned both vowel slots the same mid tone and manufactured a same-tone match; on tone-marked input, where the two vowels of such a pair almost always carry different tones, the rules would be structurally inert. Any future rule here must be tone-agnostic and needs a lexicon, not a grapheme-only condition. BENCHMARK CEILING, MEASURED NOT SOURCED: the wikipron row's PER (0.3832) understates its own error because 7.56% of the raw 4937-entry gold (373 words) is alphabet-chart noise — single letters and short digraph-name entries that transcribe trivially. Scored separately, the trivial subset gets 0.2011 PER and the 3891 real words get 0.3913 PER, a flattery gap of 0.1902; the real-word number is the one that reflects running-text accuracy. This is a DEGRADED-INPUT ceiling, not an orthographic one, and it is worth naming as its own category distinct from a language whose writing system omits tone: Yoruba orthography DOES write tone, but wikipron's scraped headwords mostly do not carry it — by this spec's own count only 32 of 4937 (0.65%) have a tone diacritic, while the IPA gold routinely wants high or low, so an orthographically unmarked (mid-tone) vowel is scored wrong whenever the gold's real tone is high or low. Folding tone and nasalisation marks out of both hypothesis and gold before scoring drops PER from 0.3832 to 0.0284 on the same 4065 words: segmental accuracy is about 97%, essentially ceiling, and the remaining error is overwhelmingly the tone-mark mismatch just described, not a segmental defect. Consistent with an input that mostly omits tone, 584 of the 4088 distinct wikipron words (14.3%) carry more than one gold IPA reading for the same spelling — evidence that the untoned input forces several tone readings onto one written string, not a score floor, since the harness scores each word against the best of its references. CONTAMINATION IN THE GOLD, NOT A SPEC GAP: of the 13 characters the wikipron 'yo' word list uses that this spec's grapheme table does not cover — c z Ɔ Ɛ ɔ ɛ Ḿ ḿ Ị ị Ộ ộ Ụ ụ, plus bare combining tone marks — none of them is Standard Yoruba orthography. ⟨ị⟩, ⟨ụ⟩ and ⟨ộ⟩ are Igbo/Vietnamese-pattern subdot and circumflex letters, ⟨c⟩ and ⟨z⟩ are not in the Standard Yoruba alphabet at all, and bare ɔ/ɛ/Ɔ/Ɛ are raw IPA or Pan-Nigerian-alphabet symbols standing in place of ⟨ọ ẹ⟩. 143 of 4088 words (3.5%, measured by running the engine and counting words with an UNKNOWN token) are affected. Together with the extended-orthography note above, this points at non-Yoruba entries inside the yor_latn_broad scrape; adding graphemes to match them would be fitting the spec to contaminated data rather than describing Yoruba, so none were added. TONE IS FULLY MODELLED: this ceiling is a property of the wikipron input, not an unhandled feature — tests/test_yoruba_tone_and_nasal_vowels.py exercises the tone, nasal-vowel and syllabic-nasal rules and passes 63/63.

Source for the open-syllable constraint, the seven-oral/five-nasal vowel inventory (no nasal counterpart of /e/ or /o/), and the statement that syllabic nasals bear tone. The document states 'Version 1.0' and no publication year; 2005 is the creation timestamp in the PDF itself, whose latest cited work is from 2002.

allophone_rules.notes: A vowel in the syllable an ⟨m⟩ or ⟨n⟩ onsets is nasal, and the orthography writes no ⟨n⟩ for it because nasality is predictable there: ⟨mi⟩ ⟨mu⟩ ⟨mọ⟩ are /mĩ mũ mɔ̃/, and ⟨n⟩ before a vowel is itself the nasal allophone of /l/, which only occurs before a nasal vowel — ⟨inú⟩ /īlṹ/ → [īnṹ] (NO citation could be retrieved for this orthographic convention: Bamgboṣe 1969, Abraham 1958 and Sachnine 1997 are all named in the sources block but none is obtainable, so the rule rests on a distribution MEASURED in the shipped wikipron/yor gold rather than on a source. Counting every gold phone that immediately follows an [m] or an [n], the vowel carries a nasal tilde in 250 of 289 tokens of /i/, 151 of 167 of /ɔ/ and 133 of 145 of /u/ — 86 to 92 per cent — while /a/ is nasal in only 102 of 190, which makes it the weakest member of the set the rule covers. Abraham 1958's dictionary is reported to write the nasality out as ⟨inún⟩, but that report is second-hand). Restricted to /i a ɔ u/: phonemic /ɛ̃/ is confined to the single SEY word ìyẹn~yẹn 'that' and the gold agrees — /ɛ/ after a nasal onset is nasal in only 3 of 55 contexts (5.45%) — so no EPSILON rule is added. Yoruba has no /ẽ õ/ either, so ⟨me⟩ ⟨mo⟩ ⟨ne⟩ ⟨no⟩ stay oral.

wikipron.measured: Yoruba orthography does write tone (acute/grave/mid), but the wikipron scrape's headwords mostly do not carry it: only 32 of 4937 words (0.65%) have a tone diacritic, so an unmarked (mid-tone) vowel is scored wrong whenever the gold's real tone is high or low. Folding tone and nasalisation marks out of both sides drops PER from 0.3832 to 0.0284 on the same 4065 words; tests/test_yoruba_tone_and_nasal_vowels.py (63/63) confirms tone itself is fully modelled. This is a degraded-input ceiling, not an unhandled feature. Restoring the display headword confirms this with a direct measurement rather than a fold: the wikipron_restored row recovers 3257 of the 4937 rows from the MediaWiki API, and on the 3249 of them the harness scores, PER falls from 0.4353 to 0.0441 and word error from 1.0000 to 0.1717 with 2691 words transcribed exactly. Restoring the tone is a weaker claim than folding it out (0.0284) because it leaves the contrast in the gold instead of deleting it from both sides, and the residual it leaves is real: downstep, which the orthography does not write, and the extended orthography's unmapped ⟨ị ụ⟩. The remaining 1680 rows are mostly pages whose untoned title is the title of several distinct words -- ⟨aba⟩ renders abà, abá, àba and àbá -- where the intended reading is not recoverable and no row is emitted.
